abstract: During perception, the brain must veridically portray sensory representations while simultaneously highlighting unexpected events. According to two-process theory of predictive perception, this balance is achieved via complementary mechanisms: precision-weighted predictions sharpen sensory tuning around expected features, while momentary surprisal scales response gain, dampening expected inputs and amplifying unexpected violations. However, standard approaches to investigate these processes, such as categorical multivariate decoding, primarily capture shifts in overall signal-to-noise, making it difficult to disentangle changes in population tuning width from modulations in response gain. Here, we combine ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) with population receptive field (pRF) modelling and a continuous Bayesian ideal observer to test how expectations dynamically modulate frequency tuning across the human auditory hierarchy. We first established static pRF preferences and tuning widths independently of predictive inference. We then separately compared this static pRF tuning against two dynamically modulated alternatives. The first model evaluated how tone-by-tone precision-weighted predictions dynamically sharpen and broaden pRF tuning width, while the second model evaluated how gain (by amplification and dampening) was modulated by tone-by-tone information-theoretic surprisal. Across primary, belt, and associative auditory cortices, both a sharpening model driven by precision-weighted predictions and a gain model driven by surprisal explained significantly more variance compared to a static baseline model. Counterfactual models inverting these driving features yielded no improvement, ruling out non-specific model mimicry. Additionally, contrasting local and global tonotopic implementations revealed a feature-selective dissociation: whereas precision-weighted predictions locally sharpened pRFs tuned to expected frequencies, surprisal acted as a global broadcast signal that multiplicatively scaled pRF gain across all frequency channels of the tonotopic map. Together, these findings demonstrate that the auditory system continuously balances selectivity for expected structure and responsiveness to surprising input through local sharpening and global gain modulation.
